A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SuffixDecoding, with matching authors, core equations and algorithm. The complete documents, including v2's technical appendices, are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial changes to the title, organization and evaluation. V1 has no appendix.

before.justification: V1 reports original hardware measurements of throughput, latency and token acceptance, plus simulated ablations and distribution-shift experiments in Section 4.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark comparisons, live OpenHands task-completion measurements, simulated ablations and dataset entropy measurements in Section 4 and Appendix A.

M1.justification: Section 3 adds hybrid decoding: each iteration first generates a suffix candidate, then falls back to a model-based speculator such as EAGLE-3 when its score does not exceed a threshold. This substantially extends the inference procedure. The original suffix trees, greedy expansion, adaptive speculation length and scoring remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds repository issue resolution through SWE-Bench/OpenHands, including live agent execution, and explicit Spec-Bench coverage of tasks such as reasoning, question answering, summarization and translation. AgenticSQL remains. WildChat, Magicoder and Spider remain in supplementary analyses, although their original hardware benchmark comparisons are removed.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates incremental decoding and SpecInfer. V2 retains vanilla decoding but replaces the SpecInfer comparison with EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3, Prompt Lookup Decoding and Token Recycling; Appendix A.1 also reports an EAGLE row. The live vLLM experiment compares against native Prompt Lookup Decoding. Citations to EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup in v1 were not evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: V1 uses Llama-3-70B-Instruct with eight-way tensor parallelism and a Llama-3-8B draft model in FlexFlow Serve. V2's main comparisons use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on one H100 with batch size 1 in Spec-Bench. Its new vLLM experiment uses a specialized 32B model, four-way tensor parallelism, prefix caching and task-completion timing that includes prefilling and agent actions.

E4.justification: V2 adds an entropy-based analysis of task predictability and SuffixDecoding suitability in Appendix A.2.3. The existing adaptive-length, global-versus-request-tree, corpus-size and distribution-shift studies remain, as does the 66-token speculation-tree example. Moving the distribution-shift study to the appendix does not add a robustness experiment.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and averages without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new entropy measurements are descriptive diagnostics rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: V1's main result tables are replaced by new benchmark and hybrid results. Appendix A.1 reports AgenticSQL Suffix (linear) speedup of 5.345× and Spec-Bench Hybrid (linear) speedup of 2.500× over vanilla decoding; Section 4.3 adds 1.8–4.5× task-completion speedups. These use changed settings, not direct improvements over v1. V2 also contains discrepancies: Section 4.2 gives AgenticSQL EAGLE-3 about 1.9× speedup and 3.6 accepted tokens, while Appendix A.1 reports 1.623× and 3.160.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2.3 adds an operational mathematical definition of task structuredness using a weighted average of suffix-tree node continuation entropies. The existing C(N), D(N), SCORE and adaptive MAX_SPEC definitions, complexity statements and underlying reasoning remain unchanged. No new theorem or proof is provided.

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes a general model-free alternative competitive across chat, coding and SQL workloads. V2 centers the contribution on fast, adaptive speculation for repetitive agentic workloads, adds hybrid decoding and live agent-completion claims, and replaces the headline SpecInfer comparisons with EAGLE-2/3 and Token Recycling comparisons. Broad standalone competitiveness on open-ended workloads is qualified.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly discusses standalone SuffixDecoding's weakness on high-entropy Spec-Bench workloads and explains why hybrid decoding helps there but adds overhead on agentic workloads. It adds agentic repetition mechanisms, entropy-based applicability guidance and qualifications about baselines failing on long contexts. V1's tree-selection failure discussion and distribution-shift interpretation are retained.

D1.justification: V2 adds an explicit ArcticInference code-release link and documents Spec-Bench/vLLM integration, the OpenHands model, prefix caching, agent configuration and iteration limits. It removes v1's detailed FlexFlow/C++ implementation description and explicit disjoint corpus/evaluation split disclosure. Some new setup descriptions remain unreconciled: main-text versus appendix RAM is 2 TB versus 1 TB, and Figure 6 specifies eight concurrent tasks while Appendix A.1.1 allows sixteen workers.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts toward speculative decoding for agents. V2 adds discussion and citations covering EAGLE-3, Token Recycling, ANPD, OpenHands, SWE-Bench, agent reasoning methods and Dynasor. It removes the separate Online Speculative Decoding discussion and expands the comparison with systems that accelerate agent workflows.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around agentic repetition and fast adaptive speculation. Background gains an agentic-algorithms discussion, evaluation is reorganized around baseline and live-system studies, and technical details and retained analyses are redistributed into appendices. This exceeds changes caused solely by added experiments.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column formatting. The original throughput/latency plots and main result tables are replaced by an aggregate benchmark figure and extensive appendix tables. V2 adds the end-to-end timing Figure 6 and entropy Table 1, while relocating or resizing retained workflow, example and ablation figures.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the agentic use case: v1's agentic evidence concerned inference measurements from one proprietary SQL pipeline, whereas v2 adds public software-engineering tasks, live task-completion timing and model-free as well as model-based comparisons. The hybrid evaluation and explicit high-entropy limitations clarify applicability. Reporting discrepancies, unreconciled settings and lost split disclosure are material drawbacks, but they do not outweigh the substantial new evidence connecting decoding acceleration to practical agent completion time.
